name: Comfrey (Symphytum officinale)
short: By mouth: case reports of liver veno-occlusive disease, one fatal, linked to its pyrrolizidine alkaloids; cancer in rodents. On the skin: a review of 26 studies found few adverse events.
text: By mouth: comfrey contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids, and a review describes the use of comfrey leaves as a substantial health hazard, with liver toxicity in humans and cancer-causing potential in rodents; the main liver injury is veno-occlusive disease (blockage of the small liver veins), which can lead to cirrhosis and eventually liver failure, and the review notes that distribution of comfrey is banned in Germany and Canada. In case reports, a 23-year-old man who had taken comfrey leaves developed hepatic veno-occlusive disease with severe portal hypertension and died from liver failure, and a 49-year-old woman developed veno-occlusive disease after regularly taking supplements containing pyrrolizidine alkaloids, mainly from a powder sold as ground comfrey root; other case reports, available only as titles, describe veno-occlusive disease after comfrey herb tea and after ingestion of comfrey. A further review of animal and laboratory work concludes that comfrey is mutagenic in the liver and causes tumours in experimental animals. In contrast, a systematic review of 11 case reports of possible pyrrolizidine alkaloid harm from comfrey or coltsfoot found that nine showed some degree of association, but uncertain identification of the plant actually taken compromised attribution, and the authors judged these cases an unreliable body of evidence on which to draw conclusions about oral comfrey. On the skin: a scoping review of 26 studies of external comfrey preparations (13 randomised trials, 5 non-randomised trials and 8 observational studies) found that few adverse events were reported and that topical application appears to be safe, but called for further rigorous assessment; in a laboratory study on donated human skin, only small amounts of the pyrrolizidine alkaloid lycopsamine, added to a comfrey cream in which no pyrrolizidine alkaloids had been detected, passed through the skin. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
